\section[il sindacato]{il sindacato — the trade union}

\label{lesson:IT-C359-sindacato}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the employer, then the Italian for the employee.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il sindacato}
\textbf{il sindacato} — \textquotedblleft{}the trade union\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Il sindacato chiede stipendi più alti.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The union is asking for higher wages.}
\end{quote}

A union member is \emph{un iscritto al sindacato}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sindacato} is built on \emph{sindaco}, a learned borrowing from Late Latin \emph{syndicus} \textquotedblleft{}a representative of a body\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from Greek \emph{sýndikos} \textquotedblleft{}one who helps in court\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{díkē} \textquotedblleft{}justice\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il sindacato}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il sindacato}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{il sindacato}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for the employer, then the Italian for the employee, then say \emph{il sindacato} again
\end{itemize}

\section[lo sciopero]{lo sciopero — the strike}

\label{lesson:IT-C359-sciopero}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the employee, then the Italian for the trade union.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: lo sciopero}
\textbf{lo sciopero} — \textquotedblleft{}the strike\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Domani c'è lo sciopero dei treni.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Tomorrow there is a train strike.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Essere in sciopero} — to be on strike. Strikes are announced in advance, so check before you travel.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sciopero} is built on \emph{scioperare}, usually traced to a Vulgar Latin \emph{exoperāre} \textquotedblleft{}to be out of work\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{ex-} \textquotedblleft{}out of\textquotedblright{} and \emph{operāre} \textquotedblleft{}to work\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{opus, operis} \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{lo sciopero}, once more

\section[scioperare]{scioperare — to go on strike, to strike}

\label{lesson:IT-C359-scioperare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the trade union, then the Italian for the strike.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: scioperare}
\textbf{scioperare} — \textquotedblleft{}to go on strike, to strike\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Gli insegnanti scioperano contro la nuova legge.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The teachers are striking against the new law.}
\end{quote}

Stress: \emph{sciòpero}, \emph{sciòperano}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{scioperare} is usually traced to a Vulgar Latin \emph{exoperāre} \textquotedblleft{}to be out of work\textquotedblright{}, built from \emph{ex-} \textquotedblleft{}out of\textquotedblright{} and \emph{operāre} \textquotedblleft{}to work\textquotedblright{}, on \emph{opus, operis} \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[il turno]{il turno — the shift; the turn}

\label{lesson:IT-C359-turno}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the strike, then the Italian for to go on strike.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il turno}
\textbf{il turno} — \textquotedblleft{}the shift; the turn\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Questa settimana faccio il turno di notte.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{This week I am on the night shift.}
\end{quote}

\emph{A turno} — taking turns. \emph{È il tuo turno} — it is your turn.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{turno} came into Italian from French, from the family of \emph{tourner} \textquotedblleft{}to turn\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), which goes back to Latin \emph{tornāre} \textquotedblleft{}to turn on a lathe\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{tornus} \textquotedblleft{}a lathe\textquotedblright{}, a Greek word: work goes round in turns.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il turno}, once more

\section[gli straordinari]{gli straordinari — the overtime}

\label{lesson:IT-C359-straordinari}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to go on strike, then the Italian for the shift.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: gli straordinari}
\textbf{gli straordinari} — \textquotedblleft{}the overtime\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Questo mese ho fatto molti straordinari.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{This month I did a lot of overtime.}
\end{quote}

Short for \emph{le ore straordinarie}. \emph{Straordinario} also means extraordinary.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{straordinari} is the plural of \emph{straordinario}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{extraordinārius} \textquotedblleft{}out of the usual order\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built from \emph{extrā} \textquotedblleft{}outside\textquotedblright{} and \emph{ōrdō} \textquotedblleft{}order\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to go on strike, then the Italian for the shift, then say \emph{gli straordinari} again
